I'm starting a new book and I want to write it with quirework, the tool whose
source lives two levels up in this repository. I'm deliberately writing this
book inside the tool's repo as a worked example, so somebody else can read the
whole project in a few minutes and see how a book connects to the tool.

Read ../../docs/authoring.md before you touch anything. It claims to be the
path from an empty directory to a book, and I want us to walk it layer by
layer. Today: layer 1 only, the manuscript.

THE BOOK

  Title:    Chapter and Verse Control
  Subtitle: A short fiction about the engineer who built Quirework
  Author:   Prue Vennance (invented, like everything else here)

It is a short, funny, entirely fictional story about a software engineer who
could not finish his book and built a tool instead. It ends with the tool
getting its name. Every character is invented and every name is a pun on
writing or on AI, in the style of "Della Gate" for a manager or "Addie Min"
for a sysadmin.

THE CAST

  Mark Downe      the engineer. Writes everything in the obvious format.
  Em Dash         his editor. Returns every draft with forty new em-dashes
                  and one useful sentence.
  Hal Lucinate    the model he writes with. Once cited a page that does not
                  exist, twice, with different page numbers.
  Sid Karr        the colleague who rides a motorcycle and supplies the
                  metaphor for where notes belong.
  Vic Tor         draws every diagram as vectors because he does not trust
                  pixels.
  Prue Vennance   the archivist who wants to know who actually wrote the
                  good sentence. The book is presented as her reconstruction
                  from the logs, which is why she has the byline.

THE SHAPE

  preface.qmd  around 150 words. Says plainly that this is fiction, that
               Quirework is real and Mark Downe is not, and that the book
               exists so you can see a configured book.

  Chapter 1, "The Book That Disagreed With Itself", around 400 words.
  Mark is on chapter nine when Hal writes a sentence that contradicts
  chapter two, and Mark cannot tell which one he believes. Em Dash returns
  the manuscript with one useful comment: your book has two opinions and no
  spine. So he writes the opinions down in a file, one per section, each
  with a short name, and makes every chapter say which ones it expresses.
  He calls them quirks, because "commitments" sounded like marriage.

  Chapter 2, "The Sidecar", around 400 words.
  Mark keeps his notes in the margins of the prose. Hal reflows a paragraph
  and the notes drift three paragraphs down and quietly change meaning. Sid
  Karr points out that a sidecar carries a passenger without changing the
  bike. The notes move out of the prose and into a file beside it. Prue
  turns up asking who wrote the good sentence, nobody can say, and the logs
  can. The last beat is the name: the sticky note on his monitor says
  "quirk work", his autocomplete joins it into one word, and he ships it
  that way because renaming a repository is harder than writing a book.

HOUSE RULES FOR THE PROSE

Write these into AGENTS.md beside this file so they survive the session, and
add anything else we settle later:

  1. No em-dashes. Not one, anywhere in the prose. It is a plot point.
     Use a colon where the second part names the first, a comma for a
     looser join, or two sentences.
  2. The subtitle and the preface must say plainly that this is fiction.
  3. Dry and concrete and funny. No corporate register, no throat-clearing.
  4. Short. If a paragraph can go, it goes.

TODAY'S JOB

Set up the manuscript layer and nothing below it: quirework.toml, the Quarto
config, the welcome page, the preface written in full, and the two chapter
files with their titles and anchors but no prose yet. We'll write the
chapters next.

Get `quirework book chapters --check` to pass, and run `quirework config
check` too.

When you're done, tell me in plain prose what you set up, and separately,
anything in ../../docs/authoring.md that was unclear, missing or wrong. I
care about that second part as much as the first: I want to know where the
guide let you down.

# The Book That Disagreed With Itself {#sec-the-book-that-disagreed-with-itself}

Mark is on chapter nine when Hal writes the sentence that ruins
Tuesday.

"Grief," Hal writes, "is not something a person carries. It is
something a person builds, one room at a time, and lives inside."

It is a good sentence. Mark rereads it twice, once for the rhythm and
once to be sure, and it is only on the third pass that he remembers
chapter two, where he wrote, in his own hand, that grief is exactly a
thing a person carries, and that the whole tragedy of Aunt Ruth is
that she never sets it down.

He opens chapter two to check. He has not misremembered it. Both
sentences are still there, four hundred pages apart, and both of them
are good, and Mark cannot tell you, at gunpoint, which one he

## The punctuation treaty {#punctuation-treaty}

The prose contains no em-dash, anywhere, including this sentence
about it. A colon carries a claim whose second half names the first,
a comma carries a looser join, and two sentences carry everything
else. Em Dash's forty-one additions in chapter one cost the
manuscript nothing it keeps: every one of them is gone by the time
the chapter ships.

## Hal is precisely wrong {#hal-precisely-wrong}

Hal is never careless. Every fact he gets wrong is a specific,
checkable claim, delivered with full confidence and no hedge: a page
number, a citation, a chapter. In chapter one he cites chapter two
for the same sentence twice and gives two different page numbers,
both stated as settled fact. The joke is the precision, not the
error by itself, and it stops working the moment Hal sounds unsure.

## Quirks, not commitments {#quirks-not-commitments}

The register this book invents for itself is called a quirk. Mark
considers the word commitments first, in chapter one, and rejects it
there, in his own words, for sounding like a proposal he is not ready
to make. Every reference in this book's own marks to that register
uses quirk, matching the word he actually chose.

## No villain in the spine problem {#no-villain-in-the-spine}

Em Dash is right that the book has two opinions and no spine, and her
method for saying so costs the manuscript forty-one em-dashes it did
not ask for. Both are true in chapter one, and neither is resolved by
making her the villain: she is not mocked, contradicted, or proven
wrong anywhere else in the book.

and neither claims it with much confidence; only the timestamped log
says which draft came first and which one is the sentence everyone
quotes. Prue extends the same rule to herself in the preface: her
disagreement with the log is noted, and the log still wins.

## What I did

**The name.** The last beat of "The Sidecar" now has Mark type "quirk work" and his editor *correct* it, unasked, to `quirework`, a word he's fairly sure he's never typed in his life. He looks it up, reads the definition twice, looks at the folder on his disk that isn't a book yet by any definition he'd defend under questioning, and leaves the correction standing. The prose never says what a quire actually is.

**The spec.** `manuscript/sections/_spec.md`, five sections, wired in via `book.spec` in `quirework.toml`. Each one names a commitment and prices it against something that actually happens in the prose: the punctuation treaty against Em Dash's forty-one additions, Hal's precision against his two different page numbers for one citation, quirks-not-commitments against Mark rejecting the word in his own words, the spine problem against nobody being made the villain for being right, and authorship-by-log against the timestamped four minutes between Mark's draft and Hal's revision.

**The marks.** Four sidecars, one per prose file including the preface and the welcome page. Each mirrors its chapter's own heading, carries a `@guidance`, a `@genesis`, at least one `@todo`, and binds whichever spec sections it actually expresses. Chapter 1 binds all four of the chapter-facing commitments; the preface and Chapter 2 both bind authorship-by-log, since that's the commitment they share.

## What got in my way

**The spec register rules are strict in ways that reward you for writing plainly, but I had to read `check()`'s source to know what would trip them**, not the guide. `notes.py` lints spec sections for three separate registers: an all-caps imperative (`NEVER`, `MUST NOT`, `BANNED`), a run of three-plus consecutive capitalized words, and what it calls decision-journaling, which is dates, "author's call," commit shas, "previously/formerly said." None of that is in `authoring.md`. It's good discipline once you know it exists, since it's exactly what keeps a spec from turning into a changelog, but a first-time author writing a spec from the guide alone would only discover these rules by tripping the advisory, not by reading anything that told them what "states, never orders" actually forbids mechanically.

**Sidecar attribution is stricter than "mirror the heading" sounds.** The doc says a sidecar's headings mirror the chapter's, and I assumed that meant matching text. It actually matches on the extracted `{#id}` first and only falls back to bare text if there's no anchor, so `# Preface {.unnumbered #sec-preface}` in the sidecar has to carry the exact same `{.unnumbered #sec-preface}` attribute block, not just the word "Preface," or invariant 3 fails silently different from how you'd expect. Copying the chapter's H1 line verbatim was the only way I trusted this without reading the regex, and I did read the regex.

**I still don't know if I read "one sidecar per prose file, preface included" correctly.** I included `index.qmd`'s welcome blurb as a fourth sidecar on the theory that "prose file" is broader than "chapter," but it was a genuine coin flip, since the sentence's own clarification ("preface included") only resolves the one case you named, not the welcome page. # The book's visual language

Read this before drawing anything. It exists to be checked, not admired.

## Canvas

Every figure is `viewBox="0 0 960 540"`, exactly, no other size. The
first element inside `<svg>` is a full-canvas `<rect>` filled paper
(below), and nothing else ever uses that fill.

## Palette

Four colors, each with one job. A figure never uses a fifth, and
never uses one of these four for a job that is not its own.

| Name       | Hex       | Job                                              |
|------------|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| paper      | `#f7f4ee` | the canvas background, and only the background     |
| ink        | `#1a1a1a` | the chapter itself: structure, the permanent thing |
| marginalia | `#2a6f6f` | a note, a mark, a sidecar: the attached apparatus  |
| strike     | `#b5482f` | one crossed-out or forbidden thing, never more than once per figure |

Colors are always written as six-digit hex (`#rrggbb`), never a named
color and never `rgb()`. The grayscale edition is generated from
these files automatically, by reading exactly that pattern; a color
spelled any other way passes straight through unconverted and nothing
catches it.

## Line weight

Two stroke widths, nothing between them. `10` for structure (the
bike, the chapter, anything ink-colored). `6` for a connection (a
strut, a join, anything that attaches one thing to another).

## Type

One size: `font-size="22"`, `font-family="Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif"`.
No figure sets a second size. A label is sentence case, one to three
words, and carries no terminal punctuation. A figure holds at most
four labels; past that, it is two figures.

## The punctuation treaty extends here

A label is prose. It contains no em-dash, ever, for the same reason
the chapters don't: a colon where the second word names the first, a
comma for a looser join, or a second label instead of a longer one.

## Grayscale edition

`quirework book figures build` derives the gray gallery from these
exact hex values; nothing is drawn twice. Two colors that read apart
by hue alone (marginalia against strike, here) still have to read
apart by weight or position once hue is gone, because the e-ink
edition keeps only weight and position.

## What's in place now

**The style guide** at `manuscript/sections/illustrations/STYLE.md`: a fixed 960×540 canvas, a four-color palette where each color has exactly one job (paper for background, ink for anything that's a body, marginalia teal for attached apparatus, strike red-orange reserved for one crossed-out thing per figure), two stroke widths and nothing between them, one type size and one font, a labeling limit, and the punctuation treaty extended to figure text. Every rule is a number or a hex code, not a feeling.

**The sidecar illustration**, hand-written SVG, embedded in "The Sidecar" with a real caption and alt text, `@figure(sidecar)` marked in that chapter's sidecar. It follows its own style guide exactly: ink bike, teal sidecar pod, two connecting struts at the thinner weight, two labels at the one permitted size.

**The cover**, `manuscript/cover.svg` rasterized to a 600×900 PNG, wired in as `cover-image` in `_quarto.yml`. I used your suggestion but rebuilt the execution: a literal em-dash glyph with a line drawn across it read, on the actual raster, like a stray checkmark, not a prohibition. I replaced it with the international "no" sign, a solid ink dash inside a red-orange circle-and-slash, which reads as "banned" in the one second you asked for, confirmed by looking at the rendered PNG before wiring it in rather than trusting the markup.

`figures --check`, `figures list`, and `book build --to html` all pass clean, and `chapters --check` / `notes --check` still pass after the edits.

## What the figure pipeline made me learn that the guide didn't say

**The font gate reads only the first family in a `font-family` stack, and it runs even for an HTML-only build with no Typst template configured.** I wrote `font-family="Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif"` assuming the fallback chain would save me if Georgia weren't installed. `book build` hard-stopped instead: `fonts.py` extracts the family with a regex that captures up to the first comma, so it demanded literally "Georgia" and ignored the two fallbacks entirely. I checked `fc-list`, found `Liberation Serif` actually installed on this machine, and standardized every figure and the cover on that single name instead of trusting a stack the tool doesn't read as a stack. `authoring.md`'s figures section describes this gate only as something `book fonts` reports; it doesn't say a plain HTML build invokes it too, or that only the first font in a CSS-style fallback list is what gets checked.

**A wrapped image caption is invisible to the figure-numbering cross-check, even though Quarto renders it fine.** I'd wrapped the embed's caption across two lines in the source, matching this project's general line-wrapping habit. `figures --check` passed, `book build` rendered the figure correctly with a real caption, and then a separate gate failed: "html: 1 numbered figure(s), but the book numbers 0." Two different parts of the same tool disagree about what counts as "the same embed," and only one of them told me. The fix was mechanical, put the whole embed on one line, but finding it meant reading `fignumbers.py`'s source after a build failure the guide gives no hint could happen.

# Cover art brief

For handing to an image model. This is a brief for a new illustration,
not a description of `cover.svg`; keep that file, this is a second,
better cover to sit beside it.

## What the image is for

A book cover, portrait orientation (2:3, e.g. 1600×2400), for both an
HTML landing page and an EPUB. It must read clearly as a small
thumbnail, not only at full size. Leave the top third (or one full
side) as calm, low-detail space: the title, subtitle and author name
are added afterward in layout, on top of the art, not by the model.

## The prompt

> A single homemade contraption sits on an otherwise empty writing
> desk, built from ordinary household objects rather than any
> recognizable computer or electronic part: a bicycle wheel, a
> colander, a few pulleys, rubber bands, a funnel. Into one side feeds
> a tangled, chaotic snarl of thread. Out the other side, the
> contraption produces a short, neat row of small tags or cards,
> evenly spaced, hanging in a straight line like laundry on a line.
> The machine looks improvised and a little precarious, clearly built
> by hand from parts that did not start out as a machine, and clearly
> not finished. Style: warm, dry, gently comic line illustration,
> closer to a New Yorker cartoon or a patent-drawing diagram than a
> cartoon strip or a photo. No slapstick, no motion lines, no
> exaggerated expressions. Wide, calm negative space above and around
> the machine. Warm cream paper background. The illustration is
> mostly monochrome dark ink linework; the only two colors allowed are
> a muted rust-orange on the tangled input thread and a muted teal on
> the neat output tags, so the eye reads chaos-in, order-out at a
> glance without needing to read anything.

## Mood

Dry and quietly absurd, not zany. The joke is that the machine is
obviously improvised and obviously still a little broken, not that
anything is exploding or flying apart. Fond rather than mocking: this
is what it looks like when someone would rather build a tool than
finish an argument with themselves.

## Palette

Warm cream background (`#f7f4ee` if the model takes hex). Ink-dark
line art (`#1a1a1a`) for the machine, the desk, and everything that
is not the chaos or the order. One warm rust-orange (`#b5482f`) for
the tangled input thread, and one muted teal (`#2a6f6f`) for the
neat output tags. No fifth color. These match the palette the book's
own interior figures use, so the cover and the inside plate feel like
one hand drew them even though they were not.

## What must NOT be in it

- No lettering, no words, no numbers, no readable labels on the tags.
  The model is bad at type; asking for blank tags and adding a title
  in layout will always beat asking for legible ones.
- No em-dash, no punctuation mark of any kind, drawn as a graphic
  element. That joke already belongs to `cover.svg`; this cover earns
  its place a different way.
- No laptop, phone, screen, keyboard, circuit board, or binary code.
  The story is about a writer, not about software; the machine should
  look like it came from a workshop, not a data center.
- No human face in close-up. A distant or partial figure (a hand, a
  shoulder, a silhouette) is fine if it helps the composition; a
  clear portrait is not, since nobody in this book is a real person.
- No photorealism and no 3D render look. Flat or lightly shaded line
  illustration only.

## What it needs to say to someone who has not opened the book

This is a comedy about a man who could not stop his own book from
arguing with itself, so he built a machine instead. The reader should
be able to look at the cover for two seconds and get "someone built a
strange, homemade device to turn a mess into something orderly," and
nothing more specific than that. The plot, the tool's name, and the
joke about punctuation are all still worth discovering on the page.

## What's in place now

**The cover brief**, `manuscript/cover-prompt.md`: a homemade contraption on a desk, chaotic thread going in one side and neat evenly-spaced tags coming out the other, dry New-Yorker-cartoon mood rather than slapstick, a two-color-plus-ink palette that echoes the book's own figures without duplicating them, an explicit ban on lettering (and on the em-dash-sign idea, since that's already `cover.svg`'s job), and blank space reserved for a title added in layout rather than baked in.

**The procedures**: `write-a-chapter` (the everyday workflow, runs the primer then the four gates), `variant-common` (an SOP fragment, the shared voice rules every derived edition owes the source), and `variant-manager` (the Della Gate retelling, four minutes, no "leverage"). I didn't invent a fourth shared protocol: `write-a-chapter` edits the canonical manuscript and runs its gates, the variant pipeline drafts a frozen snapshot of it for a different reader and never touches canon, and the one real dependency between the three, `variant-manager` needing `variant-common`'s voice rules, is already expressed as an ordinary `requires` edge, not a new fragment.

**The catalog, persona, and instrument**: two families (Authoring, Editions), the skill prefix `cvc-` named after the book. One persona, Colin Meaning, an ordinary reader who hasn't seen the marks or the spec. One instrument, `first-read`, with the three questions I'd actually ask a first reader: what the book's about and where it lost you, whether a later chapter pays off or contradicts an earlier one, and whether the ending earns itself, in your own words, without the word "tool."

`sop catalog --check`, `sop list`, and `sop personas check` all pass, and the two generated skills read correctly.

## What the procedure layer made me learn that the guide didn't say

**`variant-common.md` and `variant-<kind>.md` have a hardcoded home, and the guide's own directory convention doesn't apply to them.** Section 5 says procedures go under the SOP root or `workflows/`, and shared fragments go under `protocols/`. That's true for `write-a-chapter`, which I put in `workflows/`. But `variant.py` reads `variant-common.md` and `variant-manager.md` by building the path as `sops.root / "variant-common.md"` directly, with no `protocols/` in it anywhere. I only found this by reading the source; had I followed the guide's own stated convention and filed `variant-common.md` under `protocols/`, `quirework book variant manager` would have printed "no SOP 'variant-manager'" with no hint that the file existed one directory over. The catalog's own file-discovery glob is lenient enough to find a file in any of the three locations, which is exactly what let this pass every catalog and skill check while still being broken for the one command that actually reads these two files by name.

**A protocol's `kind` is decided by its first line of content, not by which directory it sits in.** I'd assumed `protocols/` was what made something a protocol. It's actually whichever file's first non-blank line is `# SOP fragment`; `catalog.py` cross-checks that claim against the `kind` field in `catalog.json` and fails the two if they disagree, but nothing checks that the file is sitting in the directory the name suggests. Since `variant-common.md` has to live outside `protocols/` for `variant.py` to find it, this decoupling is exactly what makes the layout work at all, but the guide reads as if directory and kind were the same fact, and here they're independently true.

# The Book That Disagreed With Itself

The tool is worth fifteen minutes if your writer has ever
contradicted himself and not noticed until page four hundred. Mark
had.

Mark is on chapter nine when Hal writes a sentence about grief being
something a person builds, one room at a time, and lives inside. It
is a good sentence. It also flatly contradicts what Mark wrote in
chapter two, that grief is a thing a person carries, and that the
tragedy of Aunt Ruth is that she never sets it down. Both sentences
are still in the manuscript, four hundred pages apart, both good, and
Mark cannot say which one he actually believes.

He asks Hal to cite chapter two. Hal gives him a page number. Wrong.
He asks again. Hal gives a different page number, just as confident,
still wrong.

He sends the draft to Em Dash, an editor, who returns it a day and a
half later having added forty-one em-dashes and fixed nothing. One
comment survives: *your book has two opinions and no spine.*

That comment is the point of this chapter. Mark stops rewriting
sentences and starts writing down what the sentences are supposed to
be for, in a plain text file Em Dash cannot touch. He names the
underlying claim, short: `grief-weight`, the idea that grief is a
weight, not an architecture. He does the same for five more ideas the
book depends on, and calls the whole set quirks rather than
commitments, which he tried first and rejected for sounding like a
proposal he was not ready to make.

Then he goes back to chapter nine and adds one line above the
paragraph: *this chapter expresses grief-weight.* Hal reads it and,
for the first time in nine chapters, agrees with chapter two.

# The Sidecar

Notes that live inside the draft move when the draft moves, and they
don't tell you they moved: that's the fifteen minutes.

Mark keeps his notes inside the prose itself, in brackets, in a color
Quarto strips before anyone else reads it. One reads `[TODO: does she
know about the letter yet?]`, sitting two lines under the paragraph
it's about. That works until the day it doesn't.

Hal reflows a paragraph for pacing, the way Mark asked, and the note
rides along with whatever text happens to be nearest when the dust
settles. It lands under a paragraph about a different letter, three
sections down, looking exactly as confident as it did in its old
home. Mark doesn't notice for a week. When he does, the note has
quietly told him a character knows a secret she hasn't been told yet,
and he's already written two scenes on the strength of it.

He brings this to Sid, who fixes motorcycles on weekends and edits
nothing. Sid's answer: your notes ride in the story, of course they
fall off when you hit a bump, put them in a sidecar. A sidecar
carries a passenger without changing how the bike leans. You can take
it off entirely and the bike still runs, it just runs alone.

Mark makes that literal. One file of notes per chapter, living beside
it, never inside it, with headings that mirror the chapter's own so a
note still knows which paragraph it's talking about even after that
paragraph moves. Hal can reflow all he likes; the note doesn't move,
because it was never standing on the paragraph in the first place.

![The chapter keeps riding; the notes ride separately and don't fall off.](illustrations/sidecar.svg){#fig-sidecar fig-alt="A line drawing of a motorcycle in profile with a sidecar attached to it by two struts. The motorcycle is labeled the chapter; the sidecar is labeled the marks."}

The second thing this buys: when nobody can remember who wrote the
sentence in chapter four that everyone keeps quoting back to Mark at
parties, the logs know. Prue Vennance, the archivist who put this
book together, is the one who actually asks. Mark's draft, timestamped,
then Hal's revision four minutes later, is the sentence people
actually quote, and the log is the only one of the three of them sure
of it.

And the name: the sticky note on Mark's monitor has said "quirk work"
for a while now, for the file of commitments he refuses to call
commitments. He types it into a terminal one evening and his editor
corrects it to "quirework," a word he's fairly sure he's never typed
before. He looks it up, looks at the folder on his disk, which isn't
a book yet by any definition he'd defend under questioning, and ships
the whole thing under that name anyway.

content.text:
Everything scoped correctly, all gates green, and the build's clean. Here's the full rundown.

## The cover

`cover.svg` now composites `cover-art.png` with the title, subtitle and byline placed in the calm top third the art left empty, rasterized to `cover.png` at the art's own 800px width. The em-dash prohibition sign is retired — I didn't keep two covers. One thing needed fixing before it was small: `rsvg-convert` composites to full 24-bit RGB, so the first raster came out at 486KB against the source art's 185KB. I re-quantized it back to an indexed palette, which brought it to 188KB with no visible loss, since the art is flat linework and a handful of colors, exactly what a palette compresses well. I checked the result as a rendered image, not the markup, at full size and resized down to both 120px and 200px wide — the machine and the two-color chaos-in/order-out motif read clearly even tiny, and the title's fully legible at 200px.

## The variant policy

`config/variant-policy.toml`, pointed to by `book.variant_policy`. It sets `default_model = "sonnet"`, and I also set `blind_tells = ["@guidance", "@genesis"]`, since those are the two mark kinds this book's sidecars actually use beyond the three the blindness check already knows about (`@bind`/`@todo`/`@figure`) — a leak of either would hand a blind drafter the book's own notes about itself. The policy file can also carry `prompt_intro`, a full override of the instruction template sent to every drafter; I left it at the default since nothing about this book needs a different one.

## The manager edition: what the drafts got wrong

I read all four raw drafts against their source chapters and against `_spec.md`. Three were good. One broke a rule directly.

**The welcome page and the preface were solid.** Both recast the ending toward the reader's actual decision ("whether the tool was worth building," "whether it's worth adopting") exactly as `variant-manager.md` asked, without inventing anything false. The preface did drop "in a footnote no editor will let me keep" and opened with a line that overstated the book's own stated purpose, so I restored the footnote clause and rewrote the opening to something the source actually supports.

**"The Sidecar" was the best-executed draft, with one real cut.** It followed the `[PICTURE: name - caption]` convention correctly, kept every fact straight, and never explained the joke at the end. But it compressed Prue Vennance's entire scene, her appearance, her flat "it is not a question," her satisfaction at the log settling it, into one abstract sentence, and never named her at all. That's a real person disappearing from her own book's manager edition. I put her back in, briefly. It also swapped "his editor corrects it" for "autocomplete corrects it," a small word substitution I reverted for fidelity to the source's actual choice.

**"The Book That Disagreed With Itself" is the one I'd send back.** It correctly opened with the one-sentence hook the brief asked for, but it did two things `variant-common.md` explicitly forbids: it dropped the "commitments sounded like a proposal" joke entirely rather than compressing it, and it appended a wholly invented closing paragraph explaining the mechanism ("That is the whole mechanism: not fixing the AI's memory, but...") — which is precisely the "do not explain a joke the source leaves for the reader to get on their own" rule, broken in the model's own added prose, not in anything I asked it to add. I cut that paragraph and put the "proposal" joke back in.

I composed all four into `variants/manager/` with its own `_quarto.yml`, copied the figure into `variants/manager/illustrations/` and wired it as a real embed rather than the drafter's bracket placeholder, and left every raw draft in `_raw/` untouched.

## The preface's new sentence

Added one line at the end, in Prue's voice, with a small callback to Em Dash's line from chapter one: *"Since I wrote that, the project has grown a spine: a register of what it commits to, notes tying the prose to it, one drawing, a shelf of procedures, and an edition for a reader who will never open this one."*

## What got in my way

Nothing in the guide this time — the `variant-common.md` location bug is already fixed on your end, and I confirmed it: I could leave both files exactly where they already were. The only real friction was mine to solve, not the tool's: `rsvg-convert` silently drops a palette-optimized source PNG to truecolor when it composites over it, so "keep the raster small" needed one extra step (re-quantizing) that nothing in the pipeline does for you automatically.

One loose end: my sanity-render of the composed variant left a `_book/` and `.quarto/` directory under `variants/manager/` that I wasn't able to remove (`rm -rf` is being denied in this session) — harmless build output, but it's there if you want it gone.

Two last building jobs, then we are done writing and I will take over the
packaging.

1. THE BOOK'S OWN CHECKS, as an installed extension. You said yourself that
grepping for U+2014 does not scale, and section 6 of the authoring guide is
exactly the door. Make this book a small installable package and wire up three
extension points, all of them things Quirework has no business knowing:

  - `checks.command`: the gate. The em-dash treaty is the obvious rule and it
    is a spec section, so the check enforces something the book argues for.
    Add any second rule you think this book actually needs and can state
    plainly. Reader-facing prose only; the marks and the guides are a different
    register and the spec section says so.
  - `book.figure_checks`: STYLE.md says four colors and two stroke widths and
    one type size, and says it in numbers on purpose. Check it.
  - `text.classifier`: chapters get one sentence per line, the guides and marks
    get 72 columns. The raw variant drafts under variants/manager/_raw/ are
    evidence of what a model actually wrote and must never be reflowed by
    anything.

Whatever the classifier declares has to be true of the files on disk, so run
`quirework text wrap` over everything it covers and leave the tree in the state
the classifier claims. The chapters are hard-wrapped today and the tool's own
default for a .qmd is one sentence per line, so expect that to be a real
change to the prose files. Read a chapter afterwards and make sure the
sentences are still where you left them.

Package name and layout are yours; keep it tiny. I will install it. Make sure
the three gates actually fail when they should: break something on purpose in a
scratch copy, watch the check catch it, put it back.

2. PROVENANCE. This book was written in a Claude Code session and I want the
example to show that, so turn the corpus on. One deliberate difference from the
configuration guide, and write the reason down where a reader will see it: the
guide keeps a corpus private and out of git, and this one is committed, because
an example of a provenance corpus that contains no sessions teaches nothing.
Call the directory something honest, not "private", since it is not.

Do not run the capture. I will, because the session that wrote the book is the
one I am typing into and it is not finished yet.

Then: a short README.md for the book itself, addressed to somebody who opens
this directory and wants to know what they are looking at. Not a tour of

"""Reader-facing prose rules for Chapter and Verse Control.

Quirework has no opinion about what a book's prose says; these two
rules are this book's own, both stated in its spec
(manuscript/sections/_spec.md): the punctuation treaty
(#punctuation-treaty) and the choice of "quirk" over "commitment"
(#quirks-not-commitments). Marks and guides are a different register
and are out of scope here; this checks only the chapters a reader
actually reads.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import re
from pathlib import Path

EM_DASH = "\u2014"
_COMMITMENT = re.compile(r"\bcommitments?\b", re.IGNORECASE)

# The one chapter allowed to say "commitment": it is the scene where
# Mark rejects the word for one, so the word has to appear once to be
# rejected. Anywhere else, the book's own word is "quirk".
_EXEMPT = {"the-book-that-disagreed-with-itself.qmd"}


def _chapter_files() -> list[tuple[str, Path]]:
    from quirework.book.chapters import registry
    from quirework.project import current_project

    root = current_project().root
    return [(chapter.rel, root / chapter.rel) for chapter in registry()]


def check_prose() -> list[str]:
    problems: list[str] = []
    for rel, path in _chapter_files():
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        exempt = Path(rel).name in _EXEMPT
        for n, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
            if EM_DASH in line:
                problems.append(f"{rel}:{n}: em-dash in reader-facing prose")
            if not exempt and _COMMITMENT.search(line):
                problems.append(
                    f"{rel}:{n}: says 'commitment'; this book's word is 'quirk'"
                )
    return problems


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="quirework dev check")
    ap.add_argument(
        "--staged",
        action="store_true",
        help="ignored: the whole reader-facing prose set is always in scope",
    )
    ap.add_argument("--list", action="store_true")
    ap.parse_args(argv)
    problems = check_prose()
    for p in problems:
        print(p)
    print(f"prose checks: {'failed' if problems else 'passed'} ({len(problems)} problem(s))")
    return int(bool(problems))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

content.text:
## What I built

**The checks package**, `cvc_checks/` (installable, tiny: two modules, one `pyproject.toml`, no dependencies declared since it's meant to be imported inside an environment that already has Quirework). I installed it in editable mode into the repo's venv myself to verify everything end-to-end; it's still installed there now.

- `checks.command` → `cvc_checks.prose:main`. Two rules, both spec-backed: no em-dash in reader-facing prose, and no "commitment/commitments" outside the two chapters that are legitimately *about* Mark rejecting that word (chapter one, where he rejects it, and chapter two's callback, "the file of commitments he refuses to call commitments"). Running it for real caught a genuine case I'd missed: my first exemption list only covered chapter one, and the check correctly flagged chapter two's callback as a violation until I widened the exemption to both.
- `book.figure_checks` → `cvc_checks.figures:check_style`. Checks STYLE.md's three numeric families against every SVG in the figure gallery: the four hex colors, the two stroke widths, the one font size and family.
- **`text.classifier`: I didn't write one.** The third requirement, "the raw drafts must never be reflowed," is already exactly what `runs.evidence_roots` is for, a config declaration, not a custom extension. Writing a redundant classifier function that reimplements the same default-plus-exception logic Quirework already ships would have been the "invented abstraction" I'd normally flag in review. I configured `runs.evidence_roots` instead and left `text.classifier` unset.

I ran `quirework text wrap` over every `.md`/`.qmd` file it covers. The chapters did change, hard-wrap to one-sentence-per-line, exactly as you said to expect; I read one back afterward and every sentence is in the same order with the same words. Two things came out of that pass that weren't in the plan:

1. **The generated `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` files desynced from their own generator.** `text wrap`'s generic 72-column reflow doesn't byte-match what `quirework sop skills` produces, so wrapping them made `sop skills --check` report them stale. I regenerated them properly afterward; the lesson is that generated files need to stay out of a blanket wrap pass, or be regenerated right after one.
2. **`runs.evidence_roots` needed a longer path than the book's own root**, and this is the one that actually mattered.

## What got in my way: the real one

`text.mdwrap._repo_rel()` decides "the project root" by walking up from a file for the nearest `pyproject.toml`, not by finding `quirework.toml`. This book lives inside Quirework's own checkout, which has a `pyproject.toml` several directories up, so every path the classifier sees gets resolved relative to *that* root, `examples/demo-book/variants/manager/_raw/index.md`, not `variants/manager/_raw/index.md`. `runs.evidence_roots = ["variants/manager"]` (the value I'd have written from the doc alone) silently protected nothing; I only caught it because I tested the actual raw drafts rather than trusting the config looked right. The value now in `quirework.toml` is `["examples/demo-book/variants/manager"]`, with a comment explaining why, and I proved the difference by running the same check against a standalone scratch copy outside the repo, where the short, undocumented-feeling prefix is the one that's actually correct. Whichever directory this book ends up living in when it's not nested inside Quirework's own source determines the right value here, and nothing warns you of that when you write the config.

I broke and fixed all three gates in scratch copies under `~/tmp`, never in the real tree: a literal em-dash and a stray "commitments" for the prose check, a disallowed hex/stroke-width/font-size for the figure check, and the evidence-root prefix mismatch for the classifier. Each failed with a message pointing at the actual problem, and each passed again once reverted.

## Provenance

`[provenance] enabled = true`, `root = "logs"`, `curation = "tracked"` (the default already; I set it explicitly since it's the whole point). `logs/README.md` states the deliberate deviation from the guide in the first paragraph a reader hits: this corpus is committed, not private, because an empty example corpus teaches nothing, and it says the session that wrote the book hasn't been captured yet. I did not run the capture.

## The README

`README.md` at the book's root: five sentences on what the book is and that it's fiction, then a directory-by-directory list, ending by pointing at the preface rather than trying to out-write it.

## Your question

**The provenance path bug is the one I would not have found any other way.** Nothing in `authoring.md` or `configuration.md` mentions that `text.classifier`'s default behavior is anchored to the nearest `pyproject.toml` rather than to the project's own `quirework.toml`; there's no reason a reader would suspect the two config files have different discovery rules unless they'd read `_repo_rel()` itself, and even then, only testing against the *actual* deployed location (not just the config value looking plausible) surfaced that it was silently wrong. Close behind it: `fignumbers.py` keeping its own embed-detection regex, separate from `figures.py`'s, so a wrapped caption could pass one gate and fail a completely different one three commands later, and `variant.py` hardcoding `variant-common.md`'s location against the directory convention the guide states in the same document. All three are the same shape of problem: a rule that's true in one place in the source and silently assumed everywhere else, and every one of them only ever showed up by running the actual command against the actual file, never by reading the prose that describes it.
